title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: Never buy a stock just because it is in an uptrend if it is far extended above its moving average support; wait for the risk-reward to reset.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein, Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets

web_blocks.title: 8.1 Stan Weinstein Stage 2 Anatomy & Multi-Timeframe Structure (1W / 1D / 4H)

web_blocks.html: As of November 20, 2026, Costco trades in a textbook Stan Weinstein Stage 2 uptrend [19, 26]. Yet the stock is short-term stretched after jumping +11.22% in one month on TradingView (+8.24% on Finviz's 1M window) and +17.29% in three months [19, 26, 27]. Q4 FY2026 results and the November 10, 2026 $30.00 special dividend sparked that surge [19, 26]. Shares closed at $1,102.15, just 1.92% shy of the $1,123.67 high and 30.58% above the $844.06 low [26, 27]. Institutional ownership stands at 75.53%, and Discount Stores breadth shows 100.0% of peers above their 200-day EMA [26, 27]. Meanwhile, 89.0% sit above their 50-day EMA, putting sector relative strength at the 92nd percentile vs. the S&P 500 [26, 27].

Multi-timeframe checks warn against chasing right now. Costco trades +7.95% above its rising 10-week EMA ($1,020.95) and +11.70% above its 50-day SMA ($986.73) [26]. It also sits +12.58% above the 200-day SMA ($979.00) and +13.30% above the 30-week SMA ($972.76) [26]. Daily RSI(14) reads 69.60 and Weekly RSI(14) reads 72.03, both near overbought levels, while 4-hour RSI(14) is 61.99 [26]. Volume hit 4.14 million shares on November 20, or 1.69x the 2.44 million 30-day average, ahead of the November 24 ex-date [26, 27]. With the U.S. market in a Downtrend (38.8% above 50-DMA, 10 distribution days), defensive money has crowded into Costco [26].

web_blocks.title: 8.2 Support Shelves, Ex-Dividend Gap Mechanics & Short-Term Trading Assessment

web_blocks.html: Short-term traders and option buyers face a key calendar event on November 24, 2026 [19, 27]. The $30.00 special dividend plus $1.30 quarterly payout will cut the share price by ~$31.30 (~2.8%) on the ex-date [19, 27]. Aside from that drop, our Stage 2 scanner places first support at the 20-day EMA ($1,063.02) [26]. The structural support buy zone spans $1,005.64–$1,078.97, anchored near the 10-week EMA ($1,020.95) and Pivot R1 ($1,054.56) [26]. Our Stage 2 invalidation stop sits at $963.22, just below the 30-week SMA ($972.76) and 200-day SMA ($979.00) [26].

Our options overlay (`options_snapshot.py`) independently stamps `WAIT_FOR_DIP_OR_IV_COOL` [26]. Implied volatility sits at 29.6%, a 1.32x premium over 20-day realized volatility of 22.4% [26, 27]. Option buyers face both pullback risk from a +11.7% 50-day stretch and IV crush after the ex-date and December 10 earnings [26, 27]. There is no short-term momentum edge at $1,102.15. Chasing an extended leader at 53x earnings in a Downtrend tape breaks both technical and valuation rules.

web_blocks.title: Technical Ceiling & Ex-Dividend Discipline
paragraphs: Stage 2 extension (+7.95% above 10-week EMA, Weekly RSI 72.03) and high IV (29.6% vs. 22.4% HV20) block chasing at $1,102.15.
Even on a pullback to $1,005.64–$1,078.97, any new buy must still clear our Chapter 9 valuation hurdle.

web_blocks.title: 8.3 Multi-Timeframe RSI Divergence & Crowded Defensive Air-Pocket Risk

web_blocks.html: Multi-timeframe RSI signals point to late-surge exhaustion. Weekly RSI(14) is overbought at 72.03 and Daily RSI(14) sits at 69.60, yet 4-hour RSI(14) has cooled to 61.99 [26]. Intraday buying thrust is fading even while shares hover 1.92% below the $1,123.67 52-week high [26]. On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, exchanges will cut Costco's price by ~$31.30 ($30.00 special + $1.30 quarterly, ~2.8%) [19, 27]. That adjustment pulls shares from $1,102.15 toward ~$1,070.85 [26]. It tests the top of the $1,005.64–$1,078.97 support zone and the 20-day EMA ($1,063.02) without making the stock cheap [26].

Stage 2 leadership in a Downtrend tape (38.8% of U.S. stocks above 50-DMA, 10 distribution days) creates 'crowded lifeboat' risk [26]. Defensive funds have piled into one 92nd-percentile leader at 53x earnings [26, 27]. Two triggers could spark a fast 10%–15% air pocket toward the 200-day SMA ($979.00) and 30-week SMA ($972.76) [26, 27]. Broad market stabilization could rotate cash into cheap cyclicals, or December 10 earnings could show mild comp or margin softness [26, 27]. With IV at 29.6% vs. 22.4% HV20 (1.32x), neither stock nor call buyers get paid for that risk [26].

book_paragraphs: Once you and I know what a business is worth, we turn to the tape—not to override fundamental value, but to see how institutional money is actually positioned and whether the crowd is paying up or panicking. On November 20, 2026, Costco's chart is a study in defensive crowding. While the broader U.S. equity market sits in a Downtrend—with just 38.8% of stocks above their 50-day moving average and 10 distribution days on the ledger—Costco closed at $1,102.15, within 1.92% of its 52-week high of $1,123.67.

By Stan Weinstein's framework, Costco is unmistakably in Stage 2. Every major moving average is sloping upward: the 10-week EMA sits at $1,020.95, the 50-day SMA at $986.73, the 200-day SMA at $979.00, and the 30-week SMA at $972.76. Industry breadth confirms leadership, with 100% of Discount Stores peers trading above their 200-day EMA. Yet leadership is not the same thing as an entry point. Costco has rallied 11.22% in a single month and 17.29% over three months, stretching 7.95% above its 10-week EMA and 11.70% above its 50-day SMA. Its weekly RSI stands at 72.03 and daily RSI at 69.60.

Volume tells you why the stock surged into this weekend: 4.14 million shares traded on November 20, nearly 1.7 times the 30-day average, as buyers positioned ahead of the November 24 ex-dividend date for the $30.00 special cash dividend. When a stock runs 11% in a month right into a major ex-dividend date, buying at the top of the candle is a classic retail trap. Even our options desk flags the same caution: implied volatility at 29.6% is 1.32 times realized 20-day volatility of 22.4%, making calls expensive right before a mechanical ex-dividend price drop.

Let us walk through the exact mechanics of what happens on the chart over the next few trading days, because novice investors often misread special ex-dividend surges. On Friday, November 20, Costco closed at $1,102.15 on 4.14 million shares—nearly 1.7 times normal volume—as dividend-capture traders and passive flows chased the stock ahead of the November 24 ex-dividend date. When the market opens on November 24, the exchange will mechanically mark Costco's price down by roughly $31.30—the $30.00 special dividend plus the $1.30 regular quarterly payout. You do not get a free $31.30 lunch; your share price simply drops ~2.8% toward $1,070.85 while you wait until December for a taxable cash distribution.

Look at what the multi-timeframe momentum indicators are telling you and me right underneath that volume spike. Weekly RSI is stretched at 72.03 and daily RSI is right at 69.60, yet the 4-hour RSI has already eased to 61.99. That negative intraday divergence—price pressing near its $1,123.67 high while 4-hour momentum rolls off—often precedes a cooling pullback. And because Costco is trading +7.95% above its 10-week EMA ($1,020.95) and +11.70% above its 50-day SMA ($986.73), there is plenty of empty air below the price.

This is why Stage 2 leadership in a Downtrend market regime is a double-edged sword. When only 38.8% of U.S. stocks are above their 50-day moving average and the tape has logged 10 distribution days, Costco acts like a crowded lifeboat. Everyone hides in the same high-certainty name, bidding it to 53x earnings. The danger of a crowded lifeboat is that if the broader market either stabilizes—sparking a rotation back into cheaper stocks—or if Costco delivers even a slightly cautious comment on December 10 earnings, there is no marginal buyer left at $1,100. The stock can drop 10% to 12% in a hurry straight back to its 200-day moving average at $979.00 and 30-week moving average at $972.76, right above our $963.22 invalidation stop.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: RESPECTING EXTENSION IN A DOWNTREND TAPE
book_callouts.text: When the broader market enters a Downtrend, institutions hide in high-certainty compounders like Costco, pushing their RSIs above 70 and their multiples above 50x. That defensive bid feels safe—until either the market stabilizes and capital rotates back into cheaper growth, or a single modest earnings miss triggers a 15% air pocket back to the 200-day moving average.

book_subsections.title: Key Technical Shelves: Where Support Lives vs. Where Value Lives
paragraphs: Technicians watching Costco will mark the first support shelf at the 20-day EMA ($1,063.02), followed by the structural Stage 2 support zone between $1,005.64 and $1,078.97, and the primary trend floor where the 200-day SMA ($979.00) and 30-week SMA ($972.76) converge above the $963.22 invalidation stop. Notice the critical distinction between technical support and fundamental value: technical support begins around $1,063–$1,079, whereas our fundamental fair value in Chapter 7 sits at $990 and our deep-value margin-of-safety zone sits below $875. When technical support lies above fundamental fair value, a disciplined analyst does not compromise valuation just because the chart is in Stage 2.

book_subsections.title: Options Implied Volatility & Event-Driven Discipline
paragraphs: Even if you never trade a single option contract, checking the options desk is one of the fastest ways to gauge whether the crowd is overpaying for short-term exposure. Right now, Costco's 30-day implied volatility sits at 29.6%, compared with 20-day realized historical volatility of 22.4%—a 1.32x implied-to-realized premium. Our options scanner independently stamps `WAIT_FOR_DIP_OR_IV_COOL` for a simple reason: option sellers are charging you an inflated volatility premium right ahead of two known calendar events—the November 24 ~$31.30 ex-dividend adjustment and the December 10 earnings report.

Put yourself in the shoes of a trader buying December calls at $1,102.15. Not only are you fighting a +7.95% extension above the 10-week EMA and an overbought 72.03 weekly RSI, you are also stepping in front of a mechanical 2.8% ex-dividend drop and elevated implied volatility that will crush option premiums the morning after earnings. Whether you express a view through common stock or options, the tape is giving you and me the exact same message as our valuation model: do not chase.
